newsitem.title: UK: UK minister denies impropriety in sleaze probe.
newsitem.headline: UK minister denies impropriety in sleaze probe.

text.p: Junior social security minister Andrew Mitchell denied on Monday that he had improperly tried to influence a parliamentary investigation of allegations of influence-peddling against ex-trade minister Neil Hamilton.
Suspicions of sleaze have dogged Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservative party and could be an important factor in Britain's looming election, which must be held by May 22.
Another minister, David Willetts, was forced to resign last month after MPs judged he had been less than frank and open in explaining his role in the investigation of Hamilton in 1994.

But Mitchell told the House of Commons' powerful Standards and Privileges Committee that he did nothing wrong in quizzing a senior parliamentary official about Hamilton's case while he was a member of the now-defunct Members' Interests Committee.
"I did not in any sense at any time try to influence the members of the Committee improperly," he said in a memo to the panel.
Mitchell was summoned to give evidence after an opposition Labour MP produced a memo Mitchell had written to the Conservatives' chief whip, or parliamentary business manager.

Labour said this was evidence that Mitchell, who was himself a whip at the time, was abusing his membership of the committee to pass on privileged information to the government that would help it to stave off any embarrassment caused by Hamilton.
Hamilton is alleged to have accepted cash in return for asking parliamentary questions on behalf of Mohammed al Fayed, owner of up-market London department store Harrods.

But Mitchell said he wrote the memo in his capacity as a whip and not as a member of the committee, which has quasi-judicial status in judging whether MPs have breached parliament's sacrosanct, age-old rules.
"Until this day I have never discussed the confidential deliberations of this committee outside the committee," he said.
Moreover, he said any MP could have made the same inquiries he did about Hamilton with the Registrar of Members' Interests.

The registrar, Roger Sands, confirmed this in a memo to the committee. "If any member (of parliament) had asked me a question in such terms...it is most unlikely that I would have refused to respond," the parliamentary official said.
